lesson.title: Going Along with the Group: Understanding Conformity
lesson.summary: Conformity is the tendency to change one's behavior or stated beliefs to match those of a group, even without a direct order to do so, and psychologists distinguish between conforming to be liked and conforming because the group's behavior seems like genuine evidence about reality.
lesson.body:
Conformity brings together the two ideas developed earlier in this unit, social norms and social influence theory, into a single, very common real world phenomenon. Where social norms describe the shared expectations of a group, and social influence theory describes the general mechanisms through which other people change us, conformity is what it looks like when an individual actually shifts a behavior or a stated opinion to align with what the group around them is doing, often without anyone issuing a direct command.

A key distinction, developed by Morton Deutsch and Harold Gerard in 1955, separates two different reasons people conform. Normative social influence occurs when a person conforms in order to be liked, accepted, or simply to avoid the discomfort of standing out, even while privately disagreeing with the group. This kind of conformity closely resembles Kelman's compliance process discussed earlier: it is often public without being genuine. Informational social influence occurs when a person conforms because they genuinely believe the group's behavior provides useful evidence about the correct answer, especially in ambiguous situations where the person is unsure what to think or do on their own. Sherif's autokinetic effect study, discussed earlier under social norms, is a good example of informational influence at work, since participants had no independent way to judge how far an imaginary moving light had traveled and reasonably treated the group's estimates as real evidence.

Researchers have identified several factors that reliably raise or lower conformity. Conformity tends to increase as group size grows, but only up to a point, typically leveling off once a unanimous group reaches somewhere around three to five members, after which adding still more people produces little additional pressure. Unanimity turns out to matter enormously: even a single other person who breaks with the majority and gives a different answer, even a wrong one, can dramatically reduce a person's tendency to conform, apparently because it is much easier to resist group pressure once you are no longer the only dissenting voice. Conformity is also generally stronger when people must state their response publicly rather than privately, and it can vary somewhat across cultures.

Conformity as a broad category sets up the next two concepts, obedience and the Asch conformity study, quite directly. Obedience, covered next, is closely related but distinct, since it specifically involves responding to a direct command from an authority figure rather than to the more implicit pressure of a group's example. The Asch conformity study, covered after that, is the single most famous experimental demonstration of conformity itself, and returning to it in depth will make the concepts introduced here, particularly normative influence and the role of unanimity, much more concrete.
